title: Federico Gonzaga Ordered a Weekend Retreat. He Got a Shrine to the Emperor Who Made Him a Duke.
standfirst: Federico II Gonzaga asked his court painter to patch up the family's horse stables into somewhere he could dine with his mistress. What went up instead took a decade, put named prize stallions on the reception-room wall, and ended in a fresco built to flatter the emperor who had just made him a duke.

sections.heading: He Asked for a Cottage. Giulio Romano Built Him a Decade-Long Project.
sections.body: In October 1524, Federico II Gonzaga rode out to a low island on the edge of Mantua's marshes with a Roman painter he had spent [two years trying to lure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giulio_Romano) away from the city that had trained him. He had already given Giulio Romano a house in Mantua and, [according to Vasari](https://www.centropalazzote.it/en/purpose-of-the-building/), one of his own favourite horses. What Federico asked for on that ride was modest: a small residence he could retire to sometimes to feast or dine for pleasure. The island was not empty ground. Around 1502 his father, Francesco II Gonzaga, had drained the marshland at what was then called Isola del Te to [build stables for his thoroughbreds](https://www.centropalazzote.it/en/the-history/), on land just outside the city walls. Giulio went away, produced a model, and came back with something nobody had asked for. Federico, Vasari says, took one look and ordered the full palazzo built on the spot. The shell went up in about [eighteen months](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_del_Te); the frescoes that made the building famous took most of the following decade to finish.

sections.heading: The Room That Says What the Palace Was Actually For
sections.body: Two of the six horses painted life-size on the walls of the Sala dei Cavalli still have their names lettered beneath their hooves: Morel Favorito, a grey, on the south wall; Dario, a lighter-coloured horse, on the north. The room was built between 1526 and 1528, years before the palace's more famous frescoed halls, and it is the most literal statement of what this ground had always been for. The Gonzaga had [bred and cared for their horses in the same stables](https://www.centropalazzote.it/en/hall-of-the-horses/) going back to Federico's father and grandfather, and Federico himself is recorded as treating a fine horse as the best gift he could give a friend or an important guest. Putting six of them on the wall of the palace's principal reception room, life-size, at eye level, under a gilded ceiling painted with roses and the family's own emblems, was not really decoration. It was a credential. A visitor who knew horses understood exactly what kind of household could afford to breed and keep animals worth commemorating in fresco rather than simply riding them.

sections.heading: The Woman It Was Built For Has No Fixed Date of Death
sections.body: Isabella Boschetti was a Mantuan noblewoman known at court as la bella Boschetta. Her father, Giacomo Boschetti, served the Gonzaga as a courtier and soldier, and her mother was [the sister of the writer Baldassarre Castiglione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_Boschetti). She became Federico's lover well before he inherited the marquisate in 1519, and by every account the palace begun in 1525 was raised specifically so she would have somewhere to entertain and receive guests. In 1531 Federico commissioned Correggio's [Danae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dana%C3%AB_%28Correggio%29), which shows the mythological princess on a bed as gold rains down on her from a cloud, apparently meant for a room in the palace built for Isabella as part of a series on Jupiter's love affairs. She had two children with Federico. And the record runs out almost as soon as it starts: no fixed year for her own death has survived, inside a building whose every room, ceiling and doorway has been catalogued, dated and argued over for five centuries.

sections.heading: The Architect Who Never Meant to Leave Rome
sections.body: Giulio Romano trained as a boy in Raphael's workshop and was one of the assistants who finished the [Vatican's Constantine frescoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giulio_Romano) after Raphael's death in 1520. Federico Gonzaga began trying to recruit him in 1522, and it took two more years of pursuit before Giulio actually moved to Mantua in October 1524. He never left again. Federico's patronage, by every account, never faltered, and Giulio remained court artist for the rest of his life, earning over 1,000 ducats a year for work that ranged from painting and architecture to hydraulic engineering and designing costumes for jousts and masquerades. Vasari singled out that last skill for praise as readily as anything Giulio built. He is also, by most counts, the only Renaissance artist Shakespeare names outright, in a stray line in The Winter's Tale — an odd kind of afterlife for a man who spent his most productive two decades building pleasure palaces for a provincial Italian court rather than working in the city where his training and his early reputation had been made.

sections.heading: A Courtyard Built to Look Like It Was Falling Down
sections.body: Walk around the courtyard at the centre of the palazzo and the classical grammar stops adding up. The spacing between the engaged Doric columns changes from bay to bay — [every wall is slightly different](https://tykokihlstedt.com/2019/08/mantua-art-architecture-i-palazzo-te.html) — and on one wall, several triglyphs in the frieze appear to have slipped down out of their proper slots, as though the entablature above them were quietly failing. The palace's other facade inverts the expected logic of load-bearing stone: the wall surface is heavily rusticated and three-dimensional, while the pilasters set against it are flat and smooth, [a reverse of what one would expect](https://tykokihlstedt.com/2019/08/mantua-art-architecture-i-palazzo-te.html) structurally. None of this was incompetence. Giulio had trained in a discipline that treated the Doric order as a fixed rulebook — the Gonzaga's own [Basilica of Sant'Andrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_of_Sant%27Andrea,_Mantua), commissioned by Federico's ancestor Ludovico III Gonzaga six decades earlier in the same city, follows Roman precedent closely enough to be taught as a model of correct classicism. Giulio knew the rules well enough to break them in front of an audience trained to notice.

sections.heading: A Room Designed to Make an Emperor's Ally Feel Small
sections.body: The Sala dei Giganti was frescoed between 1532 and 1534, floor to ceiling, with a single continuous scene drawn from [Ovid's Metamorphoses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Giants_%28Romano%29): Jupiter and the Olympian gods crushing the rebellion of the giants who tried to storm Mount Olympus. Giulio hid the room's corners behind painted rockfall so the destruction reads as one unbroken panorama, and set the viewpoint at the level of the losing side, among the falling bodies and toppling masonry. The art historian Paula Carabell has argued that the room was [designed so its architecture and decoration fuse into a single tour de force](https://daily.jstor.org/lessons-in-mannerism-at-the-palazzo-del-te/) that can surround a visitor completely enough to be frightening. The timing was not incidental: Charles V had [elevated Federico from marquess to duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_II_Gonzaga,_Duke_of_Mantua) during a visit to Mantua in 1530 and returned in 1532, and the fresco is generally read as an allegory of the emperor's own crushing of rebellion — Jupiter's victory standing in for Charles's, with Federico's palace as the stage on which the emperor's hosts showed his court exactly whose side it paid to be on.

sections.heading: The Palace Outlived the Alliance It Was Built to Flatter
sections.body: The building survived less than a century as a working ducal retreat. In 1630, during the War of the Mantuan Succession, [Mantua was sacked over three days by an Imperial army of 36,000 Landsknecht mercenaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_del_Te), and the palazzo was looted and left abandoned along with the rest of the city. It took roughly a century and a half for anyone to seriously attend to it again: in the [second half of the eighteenth century the architect Paolo Pozzo carried out restoration](https://www.centropalazzote.it/en/the-history/) of the roofs, the floors and the frescoes, undoing at least some of the damage. The building's current use has nothing to do with horses, mistresses or emperors. It is now the Museo Civico di Palazzo Te, and holds a collection of Mesopotamian art endowed by the Italian publisher Arnoldo Mondadori. The room built to awe Charles V's court now shares a roof, in the same complex, with cuneiform tablets from a civilisation that never had anything to do with the Gonzaga at all.
